newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Ex-Soviet officials vie for Moldovan presidency.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet officials vie for Moldovan presidency.

text.p: Three former senior Soviet Communist Party officials will vie for the presidency of Moldova next month in polls that could decide the future of the former Soviet republic's ties with Moscow.

A spokesman for the Central Electoral Commission said on Friday that nine candidates had registered for the November 17 electoral race in Moldova, a predominantly rural country situated between Ukraine and Romania.
Incumbent Mircea Snegur, elected in December 1991, parliament Chairman Petru Lucinschi and Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli are viewed as clear favourites.
A recent poll by pollsters Fact, showed that 40 percent supported Snegur, while 29 percent preferred Lucinschi and 20 percent backed Sangheli.
If no candidate gets an overall majority on November 17, a second round will be held on December 1.
"The decisive word will be said by rural voters," Fact said. "The opinion of the Moldovan village has so far been little studied, and therefore is absolutely unpredictable."

The favourites were born into peasant families in Moldova's north and were top Communist Party apparatchiks in Soviet days. Lucinschi was a top member of the policy-making Central Committee before the banning of the party after a failed 1991 hardline coup. He then withdrew to Moldovan politics.
Moldova remains heavily dependent on Moscow for energy and raw materials though it has drawn closer to Romania.
Snegur, 56, is backed by his centre-right Party of Revival and Harmony, the pro-Romanian Popular Front and a group of minor nationalist parties.

Sangheli, 52, who calls himself a centrist, has the backing of the Moldova's ruling Agrarian Democratic Party, which has been at odds with Snegur the president set up his own party in June last year and accused the Agrarians of being anti-reform.
Lucinschi, 56, calls himself a social democrat and is running as an independent. Several minor leftist parties have supported his candidacy.
Analysts in Chisinau say the three leaders running for president have three different visions of Moldova's future.
Snegur wants closer ties with the West and "spiritual and economic integration" with Moldova's ethnic kin in Romania.
But presidential aides say Snegur's alliance with the pro-Romanian nationalists is only temporary, and that the president remains pro-independence.
Snegur says he would change "the incompetent Agararian government" if he is re-elected.
"My programme provides for...the enforcement of presidential power by constitutional means," he said in a radio address.

Pro-Moscow Sangheli says he needs the presidency to finish radical market reforms. "People must be fed, houses heated in winter, and gas supplies, as well as electricity, should not be interrupted," he said.

Sangheli, whose energy-poor country imports from Russia most of its needed energy resources, has developed close ties with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Rem Vyakhirev, chief executive of Russia's gas concern Gazprom.
Analysts say Sangheli's links with Russia and cool attitude to Romania are attractive to many Russian-speakers, who account for 35 percent of Moldova's population of 4.35 million.

The rebel pro-Russian 700,000-strong Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 fearing Moldova would merge with ethnic kin in Romania, has said it would not take part in Moldova's elections and would elect its own president on December 22.
Lucinschi wants equally close ties with East and West and says his political credo is "European social democracy".
He has support in the cities, but newspapers say he will struggle in the countryside, where more than 50 percent of Moldova's population live.
The other candidates include a communist, a nationalist and several independents.
